question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?

forecasts.reference-class: Earned settlement framework: proposed 10-year baseline qualifying period for settlement (ILR) for most migrants, assessed under four pillars (character, integration, contribution, residence) with potential reductions via a time-adjustment model; part of the 2025 White Paper and subsequent consultation.

sources.claim: The government announced more details on 20 November 2025; the baseline qualifying period for many migrants would be ten years, with some people able to qualify sooner or take longer.
The proposed time-adjustment model would set a 10-year baseline for most migrants, with possible shorter paths for high earners or public service workers; implementation aimed for April 2026.
Explanatory memorandum accompanying HC 1333 describes immigration-rule changes connected to the earned settlement framework.
Long residence currently requires 10 years; provides background anchor for 10-year residence concepts in UK settlement law.
Overview of the earned settlement framework: 10-year baseline for most routes, with absences, contribution, and integration considerations; consultation ongoing.
The government states default qualifying period for settlement will increase from 5 to 10 years, with exceptions.
Guidance shows a 10-year qualifying period for long residence, counting time across routes.
Parliament's Library summarises the 2025-26 reforms, including a baseline 10-year period and an April 2026 change window.
Earned settlement consultation launched November 2025; settlement to be earned rather than automatic after a fixed period.
Consultation closed February 12, 2026; officials signal major changes ahead, with potential April 2026 changes.
NHS Employers report the earned settlement consultation is underway, with April 2026 as an earliest change window.
The Earned Settlement consultation states the default qualifying period for settlement will be 10 years, with potential reductions based on contributions and other factors.
House of Commons Library notes that the 10-year baseline is proposed in the 2025 immigration policy package, with a consultation that runs until 12 February 2026.
e-petitions discuss opposition to the 10-year ILR proposal; government states no decision has been taken yet on applying changes to people already in the UK.
Long residence currently requires 10 years of continuous lawful residence, providing baseline context for a 10-year threshold in settlement rules.
Law firm notes that the consultation closes February 12, 2026 and changes could take effect as early as April 2026.
Industry summary indicating the Earned Settlement reforms would raise the standard qualifying period to 10 years with a time-adjustment model.

causal-factors.name: Baseline ILR/earning settlement default set to 10 years
causal-factors.rationale: Government documents explicitly propose increasing the standard qualifying period for settlement to 10 years and applying a time-adjustment model; implementation widely signaled for April 2026, with the policy framework also emphasizing earned contributions. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/earned-settlement/a-fairer-pathway-to-settlement-statement-and-accompanying-consultation-on-earned-settlement-accessible))

causal-factors.name: Time-adjustment model could shorten the period for some groups
causal-factors.rationale: The Earned Settlement framework includes a time-adjustment mechanism that could shorten the baseline for high earners, public service workers, volunteers, etc., depending on contributions; this partially offsets a universal 10-year baseline. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/earned-settlement/a-fairer-pathway-to-settlement-statement-and-accompanying-consultation-on-earned-settlement-accessible))

causal-factors.name: April 2026 implementation window signaled
causal-factors.rationale: Official sources indicate changes could begin in April 2026, creating a plausible path to changes before May 2026. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cdp-2026-0006/))

causal-factors.name: Consultation momentum and February 2026 closure
causal-factors.rationale: The consultation closed in February 2026 with ongoing debate; government responses acknowledge potential apply-to-existing-UK cases but without final decisions yet, sustaining the momentum toward reform. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cdp-2026-0006/))

causal-factors.name: Long-residence anchor supports 10-year frame
causal-factors.rationale: UK guidance confirms long residence is 10 years and counts across routes, which provides background support for a higher baseline in settlement rules. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/long-residence/long-residence-accessible))

causal-factors.name: NHS/employers engagement signals policy adoption
causal-factors.rationale: NHS Employers and related bodies have engaged with the earned settlement consultation and are preparing responses, signaling organizational alignment with policy shifts that can accelerate adoption; the consultation closed 12 February 2026. ([nhsemployers.org](https://www.nhsemployers.org/news/consultation-earned-settlement?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: Official policy movement toward Earned Settlement baseline (10-year baseline for ILR)
causal-factors.rationale: The November 2025 government statement and accompanying consultation explicitly propose raising the baseline qualifying period to 10 years under an Earned Settlement framework, signaling a high-likelihood shift for new settlement rules.

causal-factors.name: Implementation timing signals (possible start in April 2026)
causal-factors.rationale: Multiple official materials and credible reporting indicate changes could be introduced as early as April 2026, making May 2026 likely to reflect at least some effects for new applicants.

causal-factors.name: Transitional protections for those already on a settlement path
causal-factors.rationale: Public-sector and employer voices emphasize transitional arrangements to shield current applicants, which reduces but does not negate near-term disruption.

causal-factors.name: Sector concerns and potential refinements (health/social care)
causal-factors.rationale: NHS employers and sector groups warn of workforce impact and advocate exemptions or adjustments, potentially slowing or altering the baseline.

causal-factors.name: Parliamentary/legislative process risk of delay
causal-factors.rationale: Final Immigration Rules require parliamentary approval; delays or amendments could push changes beyond May 2026 despite initial signaling.

causal-factors.name: Earned settlement framework establishing a 10-year baseline (time-adjustment model)
causal-factors.rationale: Official materials explicitly propose a 10-year baseline with a time-adjustment mechanism to reward contributions, with implementation signals pointing to an April 2026 start for changes to permanent residence (Sources: GOV.UK A Fairer Pathway to Settlement, Updated Nov 2025; Commons Library CBP-10267, Feb 2026).

causal-factors.name: Implementation window starting April 2026 for changes to permanent residence
causal-factors.rationale: The Commons Library briefing notes that changes to permanent residence are planned to begin in April 2026, indicating near-term enactment of the 10-year baseline for new applicants (Source: Commons Library CBP-10267).

causal-factors.name: Transitional arrangements for existing migrants undecided
causal-factors.rationale: Parliamentary materials show no decision yet on applying the changes to people already in the UK, implying potential transitional protections that could delay universal application (Source: Commons Library CDP-2026-0006).

causal-factors.name: Exemptions/accelerations for high earners or public service roles
causal-factors.rationale: The policy design contemplates accelerated paths for certain cohorts (e.g., high earners, health and public service workers) via reductions under the time-adjustment model, raising the likelihood of earlier settlement for some groups (Sources: GOV.UK A Fairer Pathway to Settlement; CBP-10267).

causal-factors.name: Parliamentary debate and public petitions signaling political scrutiny
causal-factors.rationale: Active e-petitions and debate on indefinite leave to remain signal ongoing political scrutiny, which could slow or alter final policy design (Source: Commons Library CDP-2026-0006).

causal-factors.name: Fiscal/contribution-driven rationale reinforcing 10-year baseline
causal-factors.rationale: The earned settlement framework emphasizes sustained fiscal contribution, which supports raising the baseline period and is reflected in the consultation's focus on fiscal considerations (Sources: GOV.UK A Fairer Pathway to Settlement; Annex on Settlement Forecast Methodology).
